1177.title: The quiet successor's words
1177.hook: Guru Angad's saloks, short verses, sit inside the Vars
1177.howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Angad's saloks when the Vars are sung in kirtan, especially Asa di Var in the morning, where his saloks sit beside those of Guru Nanak.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nanak's way: outward things turned inward, and the name Nanak carrying on into the next voice.

Guru Nanak's voice fills raga after raga of the Guru Granth Sahib, hymn after long hymn. Go looking for the second Guru's, and it arrives another way: in small pieces, a few lines each, tucked into the Vars, the ballads, between the stanzas. Each carries a small heading: Mahala two, the second voice. This is Guru Angad, the disciple Guru Nanak chose to follow him, and in the stories about him, a man of few words and much service. The first thing to notice is how small each piece is.
screen: `NOT LONG HYMNS.` → `SMALL PIECES IN THE BALLADS.` → `MAHALA TWO: THE SECOND VOICE.`

segments.voice: A salok is a short verse of a few lines, set in the Vars before the longer stanzas, like a sharp word before a speech. That's where Guru Angad's verses live. What can a few lines hold? Here's one from the Var in Majh, the ballad this path just closed, in paraphrase. To see without eyes. To hear without ears. To walk without feet. To work without hands. To speak without a tongue. This way, a person dies while still alive. Nanak, recognize the divine order, and meet your Master. Notice the signature: Nanak, though it's the second Guru speaking. That's the name carrying on. And notice the form. Five short pictures, each impossible on its face, stacked one after another. One line to turn them: this is dying while alive. One line to point the way: recognize the hukam. Some Sikh teachers read it as a picture of living without ego: seeing, hearing, working and speaking, but no longer driven by the self that wants to own it all. The verse doesn't explain that. It leaves the five pictures hanging and lets you work them out. That's the quiet successor's style: something small and dense, the way a seed is small, left to open in you over a long time. That's today's line: few words, deep.
screen: `A SALOK: A FEW SHARP LINES.` · `SEE WITHOUT EYES, WALK WITHOUT FEET.` · `DYING WHILE ALIVE.` · `SMALL, DENSE, LIKE A SEED.` · then, large: `FEW WORDS, DEEP.`

segments.voice: Take just one picture from the salok, whichever stays with you, hear without ears, maybe, or work without hands. Keep that phrase in front of you as your breath slows, and turn it over the way you'd turn a stone in your palm, without trying to solve it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
The quiet successor's words. Guru Angad's saloks, marked Mahala two, a few dense lines each, set inside the ballads of the Granth. Today's word.
Your line: few words, deep. A seed is small, and it takes its time. See you tomorrow.

1178.title: A hundred moons, a thousand suns
1178.hook: one of his saloks says all is darkness without the Guru
1178.carry: the guru's light shows the way
1178.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok when Asa di Var is sung in the morning at the gurdwara, and Sikh teachers use it to speak of the Guru's guidance, through the Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the quiet successor's words: Guru Angad's saloks, see without eyes, walk without feet. Your line was few words, deep.

A snowfield at midday. Light pours down from the sky and bounces back off the snow until everything is one bright white. You can see perfectly well. But the trail markers are buried, and you have no idea which way the path goes. Plenty of light. No direction. The light that fills your eyes and the light that shows you the way are not the same thing. Guru Angad has a salok built on exactly that difference, and the picture is enormous.
screen: `A SNOWFIELD AT MIDDAY.` → `PLENTY OF LIGHT.` → `NO DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: The salok sits in Asa di Var, the ballad sung in the morning at the gurdwara, marked Mahala two. In paraphrase: if a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns appeared, even with all that light, without the Guru there would be pitch darkness. Stop on the size of that. A hundred moons, a thousand suns, more light than any sky has held, and still not enough. So he can't mean light for the eyes. He means the light that shows a person where they are and which way to go: what's true, what's ego, what's worth a life. In Sikh teaching, that light comes from the Guru. And who is the Guru? For Sikhs, the Gurus in their lifetimes, and now the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word itself. Earlier this year, in the Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak said the Word is the Guru. Guru Angad's salok shows what that Guru does. It doesn't add brightness to a world already full of it. It turns a different kind of darkness into sight. It's easy to assume more is the answer: more information, more options, more light on the screen. This verse quietly says no. You can be flooded with light and still be in the dark. What changes things isn't how much you can see, but whether something guides your seeing. That's today's line: the Guru's light shows the way.
screen: `A HUNDRED MOONS, A THOUSAND SUNS.` · `STILL, PITCH DARKNESS.` · `THE LIGHT THAT SHOWS THE WAY.` · `NOT MORE LIGHT, BUT GUIDED SIGHT.` · then, large: `THE GURU AS LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Remember a time you had plenty of information and still didn't know which way to go, then remember what helped you see: a teacher, a line from a text, a parent, a friend, a hard lesson. Hold that one clearly, with thanks, for a few slow breaths. If you pray, thank the Guru and say Waheguru on each breath out.
The Guru as light. Guru Angad's picture: a hundred moons and a thousand suns, and still darkness without the Guru, the light that shows the way. Today's word.
Your line: the Guru's light shows the way. A hundred moons can't do what the Guru does. Go gently.

1179.title: On service
1179.hook: he warns against service mixed with pride
1179.howItsDone: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara and beyond: cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning, and looking after the shoes of the sangat, ideally without seeking notice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the guru as light: a hundred moons and a thousand suns, and still darkness without the Guru.

A bundle of grass, cut for the cattle, soaking wet and caked with mud. Someone has to carry it home on their head. In the story Sikhs tell, Guru Nanak asks who will take it. His sons have reasons not to. Then a newer disciple, a man named Lehna, dressed in fine clothes, lifts the dripping bundle onto his own head. Mud runs down his face and into the cloth. He carries it anyway. Lehna would become Guru Angad. And when he wrote about service, he warned about a quieter danger, the one that can ride along on any good deed.
screen: `A BUNDLE OF WET GRASS.` → `LEHNA LIFTS IT.` → `A QUIETER DANGER.`

segments.voice: In Asa di Var, the morning ballad, there's a salok marked Mahala two, Guru Angad's voice. In paraphrase: a servant who serves with pride, and argues while he does it, and talks on and on, does not win the Master's favor. But one who loses himself and serves is given some honor. Nanak, he meets the One he is devoted to, and his devotion is accepted. Look at the three things it names: pride, arguing, talking too much. None of them stop the work. The dishes still get washed, the floor still gets swept. The problem is what rides along on top. Pride says, look who's helping. Arguing says, I'd do it differently and you should know. Talking says, let me tell you what this cost me. Each one turns service back toward the self. The second half is plain: lose yourself and serve. Not lose the work; lose the self in it. Then honor comes, not from the people watching but from the Master. In Sikh life this is seva: cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning shoes at the gurdwara door. And the Lehna story fits the salok exactly. He made no speech about the muddy grass. He didn't mention his ruined clothes. He just carried it. That's today's line: serve plainly.

segments.voice: Picture one small service you'll do today, for family, a coworker, a stranger, and notice which of the three would most like to come along: the pride, the arguing, or the telling everyone afterward. Don't scold it; just see it, and picture setting it down at the door before you go in. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
On service. Guru Angad's warning: service done with pride, arguing and too much talk loses its way; lose yourself and serve, and it is accepted. Today's word.
Your line: serve plainly. The work is enough, without the story about it. See you tomorrow.

1180.title: On ego
1180.hook: he calls ego a deep illness with a cure inside it
1180.howItsDone: Sikh teachers speak of haumai, ego, as a central obstacle in Gurbani, and draw on this salok from Asa di Var when they speak of its cure through the Guru's Word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, serve plainly: Lehna and the muddy grass, and a salok that warns against pride riding on service.

Where would you look for the cure to an illness? The pharmacy, the doctor's, a lab somewhere. Almost never inside the illness itself. Yesterday's salok named pride as the thing that spoils service. Today Guru Angad goes under pride to the root it grows from, what Sikhs call haumai, ego, the sense of I and mine. He gives it a hard diagnosis. Then, in the same breath, he says something no doctor's chart would say: the medicine is in there too.
screen: `WHERE IS THE CURE?` → `UNDER PRIDE: HAUMAI.` → `THE MEDICINE IS IN THERE TOO.`

segments.voice: The salok, in Asa di Var and marked Mahala two, describes ego the way you'd describe a creature's habits. This is the nature of haumai: in ego, people act. In ego they are bound, and in ego they keep coming and going. Then the turn, in paraphrase. Haumai is a long, deep illness, but its medicine is also within it. If the One shows grace, a person lives the Guru's Word. Nanak says: listen, people, this is how the troubles depart. Three things to notice. First, he doesn't pretend ego is small. It's a long illness, deep and lasting, not a bad mood that passes by evening. Second, he doesn't send you far away for the cure. The medicine is within it, and readers hear that in more than one way. Some hear that the cure is inside the person who has the illness; you don't have to become someone else to heal. Some hear that it's inside the illness itself: the same I that grabs and insists can be the I that turns and listens, its energy turned toward the Word. Third, he names how the turning happens: grace, and then living the Guru's Word, not just knowing it, day after day. So the salok is hard and hopeful at once. Hard, because it takes ego seriously. Hopeful, because the way out isn't somewhere you can't reach. That's today's line: the cure inside.
screen: `IN EGO, PEOPLE ACT.` · `A LONG, DEEP ILLNESS.` · `ITS MEDICINE IS WITHIN IT.` · `GRACE, AND THE WORD LIVED.` · then, large: `THE CURE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Let the I-thoughts come up as they do, I'm right, I'm tired of this, nobody noticed what I did, I need, and instead of fighting them, label each one softly as it passes, there's the I, and let it go by. Watch with the patience you'd give someone recovering from a long illness, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
On ego. Guru Angad's salok: haumai is a long, deep illness, and its medicine is within it, found through grace and the Guru's Word lived out. Today's word.
Your line: the cure inside. A long illness, and a medicine close at hand. Until tomorrow.

1181.title: Guru Angad close
1181.hook: the second Guru taught the script, the body and a few sharp lines
1181.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Angad in the ardas and on his gurpurab, read his saloks within the Vars, and tell of Mata Khivi's langar when they speak of the free kitchen's history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cure inside: haumai, a long, deep illness, with its medicine within it. Today this stretch with Guru Angad comes to a close.

A patch of packed earth where young men wrestle in the early morning, dust on their shoulders. A page of letters copied out in a careful, rounded hand. A long row of people sitting on the floor, being handed bowls of rice pudding. And a handful of short verses, tucked into the ballads of the Granth. Four pictures, one life. Tradition connects each of them to Guru Angad, the quiet successor: the script, the body, the kitchen, and the few sharp lines.
screen: `A WRESTLING GROUND, A PAGE OF LETTERS.` → `A ROW OF BOWLS.` → `A FEW SHORT VERSES.`

segments.voice: Start with the letters. Tradition says Guru Angad gave shape to the Gurmukhi script and taught it, so ordinary people could read and write the Gurus' words in their own language. Then the body. Tradition says he set up wrestling grounds at Khadur and encouraged exercise and strength. A healthy body, in this telling, isn't a distraction from the spiritual life; it's part of a life that can serve. Then the kitchen, and here the Granth itself speaks. In a ballad by the bards Satta and Balvand, his wife, Mata Khivi, is praised, in paraphrase, as a good woman who gives shade like a tree full of leaves. In the langar, it says, wealth is shared out, and rice pudding with ghee is served, sweet as nectar. And then the lines themselves, from these four days. See without eyes, walk without feet. A hundred moons and a thousand suns, and still darkness without the Guru. Service spoiled by pride. Ego as a long illness, with its medicine inside. Put it together and a style shows. Nothing wasted. A script so people could read. A body kept ready. A kitchen that feeds. And verses short enough for the palm of your hand, sharp enough to still cut through. That's what the second Guru left: not volume, but edge. That's today's line: short and sharp.
screen: `THE LETTERS: GURMUKHI TAUGHT.` · `THE BODY: WRESTLING AT KHADUR.` · `THE KITCHEN: MATA KHIVI'S LANGAR.` · `THE LINES: SHORT, AND STILL CUTTING.` · then, large: `SHORT AND SHARP.`

segments.voice: Let this week's pictures pass by, the muddy grass, the hundred moons, the illness with its cure, and ask what one thing you've learned lately, about your work, your people or yourself. Guru Angad close. The second Guru: tradition credits him with the script and the wrestling ground, the Granth praises Mata Khivi's langar, and his saloks are few lines that cut deep. Today's word.
Your line: short and sharp. Tomorrow, the old Guru's voice. That's today, done.

1182.title: Ego and the Name can't share a room
1182.hook: Guru Amar Das wrote many hymns on ego, the Word and the mind
1182.carry: ego and the name can't share one room
1182.tomorrow: You are the form of light
1182.howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Amar Das's hymns, headed Mahala 3, in kirtan at the gurdwara and in daily prayer: the Anand Sahib, which he composed, is part of the daily banis and is sung at the close of gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Guru Angad's few, sharp lines, and your line was short and sharp. Today, a new voice.

A page of the Guru Granth Sahib, and above the hymn, a small heading: Mahala three. The signature in the verses is still Nanak. But the voice has changed. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Amar Das as a man who came to the Guru late in life, carried water before dawn for years, and became Guru as an old man. Guru Angad spoke in short verses. His successor's hymns keep circling three things: ego, the Word, and the mind.
screen: `MAHALA THREE.` → `A LATE ARRIVAL, A LONG SERVICE.` → `EGO, THE WORD, THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Start with one line from the Var in Raga Vadhans, paraphrased: ego and the Name are opposed to each other; the two do not dwell in one place. That's the whole map in a sentence. Ego, in Punjabi haumai, is the feeling of I, I, mine, mine, the self at the center of every room. The Name, and the Word that carries it, is the Guru's teaching living in you. And the place where they can't live together is the mind, the man. Picture a small house with room for one guest: ego has the room, or the Word has it. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't call the mind bad. He talks to it, again and again, the way you'd talk to someone you love who keeps wandering off. In the Anand, his song of bliss, he says, again paraphrased: O my mind, stay always with the Lord. That's not a scolding. It's a call home. And the way home, in his hymns, is the Word. Not willpower, not cleverness: the Guru's Word, heard, sung and remembered, until it takes the room where ego used to sprawl. Some readers hear in this a man who served a long time before anyone called him Guru. He knows how ego dresses up, even inside service, and that the mind doesn't settle because you tell it once. So he says it more than once, patiently. That patience is the old Guru's voice.

1183.title: You are the form of light
1183.word: You are the form of light
1183.hook: man too jot saroop hai: O mind, you are the form of light; know your origin (Asa M3, ang 441)
1183.howItsDone: This line of Guru Amar Das from Raga Asa is often sung in kirtan and quoted in katha at the gurdwara; some Sikhs keep it as a reminder when they recite or reflect on their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the old Guru's voice: Guru Amar Das, patient with a wandering mind, saying ego and the Name won't fit in one place.

Man too jot saroop hai. A short run of Punjabi that lands like a hand on the shoulder. Guru Amar Das has been talking to the mind like someone who keeps drifting off. Here he stops calling it home for a moment and tells it what it is. Not a problem to fix. Not a list of failures. A form of light. The line is in Raga Asa, on Ang four hundred forty-one of the Guru Granth Sahib, and it opens by speaking to the mind directly: man too. O mind, you.
screen: `MAN TOO JOT SAROOP HAI.` → `NOT A PROBLEM TO FIX.` → `O MIND, YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, paraphrased: O my mind, you are the very form of light; recognize your own origin. Jot is light, the same word Sikhs use for the light that passed from Guru to Guru. Saroop is form, likeness. Mool is root, origin, where something starts. So the line holds a picture and an instruction. The picture: underneath the noise, you are light. The instruction: go find where it came from. The hymn goes on, again paraphrased: O mind, the Lord is with you; through the Guru's teaching, enjoy that love. Recognize your origin and you'll know your Lord, and understand dying and living. Notice the order. It doesn't say you are the Lord, so stop looking. It says you are light, so look for the source of the light. Knowing yourself and knowing your Lord turn out to be one road. That fits the week behind us. Guru Angad called the Guru a light in the darkness, warned that service can carry pride, and called ego an illness with its cure inside. Guru Amar Das said ego and the Name can't share a room. And now, the reason the room is worth clearing: what lives there is light. Some readers hear this line as the quiet center of all the warnings. They aren't there because the mind is worthless. They're there because it's made of something precious, and keeps forgetting.
screen: `JOT, SAROOP, MOOL.` · `LIGHT, FORM, ORIGIN.` · `KNOW YOUR ROOT, KNOW YOUR LORD.` · `WHY THE WARNINGS MATTER.` · then, large: `YOU ARE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Let the words ride the breath: in, man too jot saroop hai; out, know your origin. You don't have to work out what it means, only turn toward where your life came from and stay there gently, and if a harsh thought about yourself shows up, set it beside the line and let the line be louder. If you pray, Waheguru can take the out-breath instead.
You are the form of light. Man too jot saroop hai: O mind, you are the form of light; recognize your origin. Today's word.
